title: Data Structures & Algorithms in Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: DSA questions in Go interviews test two things simultaneously: CS fundamentals (Big-O, common algorithms) and your ability to write idiomatic Go. Interviewers notice if you write Python-style loops in Go or ignore Go's standard library tools like `sort.Slice` and `sort.Search`. For freshers, the goal is to solve classic problems correctly AND show you know Go well enough to write them the way a Go developer would.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three Go-specific DSA facts interviewers test:

- **Go has no built-in stack, queue, or linked list** — you implement them with slices (for stack/queue) or structs (for linked list). This is intentional; slices are efficient enough for most use cases.
- **`sort.Slice` takes a less function, not a comparator returning int** — `sort.Slice(s, func(i, j int) bool { return s[i] < s[j] })`. Coming from Java's `Comparator.comparingInt`, this takes adjustment.
- **Maps are Go's go-to for frequency counting and lookup** — `make(map[T]int)` for counting, `make(map[T]bool)` or `make(map[T]struct{})` for sets. The `v, ok := m[key]` pattern is essential for two-sum and similar problems.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Big-O with Go** — slice `append` amortised O(1); slice index O(1); map get/set average O(1); `len()` O(1) for slices, maps, strings; sort O(n log n)
- **Slice as stack and queue** — stack: `push = append(s, v)`, `pop = s[len(s)-1], s = s[:len(s)-1]`; queue: `enqueue = append(s, v)`, `dequeue = s[0], s = s[1:]` (O(n) — use a circular buffer or channel for production)
- **Linked list in Go** — `type Node struct { Val int; Next *Node }` — traverse with `curr := head; for curr != nil { curr = curr.Next }`
- **Sorting in Go** — `sort.Ints(s)`, `sort.Strings(s)` for simple cases; `sort.Slice(s, func(i, j int) bool { ... })` for custom order; `sort.SliceStable` when equal elements must preserve original order
- **Binary search in Go** — `sort.Search(n, func(i int) bool { return s[i] >= target })` returns the leftmost index where condition is true
- **Two-pointer pattern** — `left, right := 0, len(s)-1; for left < right { ... }` — standard Go idiom, uses simple index variables
- **Hash map patterns** — frequency count: `freq := make(map[rune]int); for _, c := range s { freq[c]++ }`; set membership: `seen := make(map[int]bool); if seen[v] { ... }`

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Queue dequeue is O(n) with a slice** — `s = s[1:]` re-slices but does not free the memory of the first element. For a production queue, use a channel or a circular buffer. In an interview, implement it with a slice and mention this trade-off.
- **`sort.Slice` comparator is a less function, not compare** — it returns `true` if `i` should come before `j`. A common mistake is writing `return s[i] - s[j]` (Java style) which is a type error in Go.
- **`sort.Search` finds the insertion point, not the element** — you must check `i < n && s[i] == target` after calling it. It returns `n` if the target is beyond all elements.
- **Map as set uses `struct{}`** — `make(map[int]struct{})` uses less memory than `map[int]bool` because `struct{}` takes zero bytes. In an interview, mentioning this shows Go-specific knowledge.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In Go, I implement stacks and queues using slices — push with `append`, pop by reslicing. For sorting, I use `sort.Slice` with a less function that returns true when element i should come before element j. For hash map problems like two-sum or frequency counting, I use `make(map[KeyType]ValueType)` and the `v, ok := m[key]` pattern to check existence without triggering a zero-value false positive. Go's map access is average O(1) and its slice operations are amortised O(1) for append."*
